title: The Philosopher's Path on Foot
blurb: Walk the Philosopher's Path under the real sun: from Ginkaku-ji along the canal and its cherries, past Honen-in and Eikan-do, to Nanzen-ji's gate, the brick aqueduct and the Keage Incline.

travel.name: The Philosopher's Path 哲学の道
Keage Incline 蹴上インクライン

npcs.name: Haruka 遥
idle: Nishida Kitaro walked this path every day, thinking. Now it's mostly us, thinking about lunch.
In early April you can hardly see the water for the petals.

npcs.name: Mr. Kenji 健二
idle: This water comes from Lake Biwa, through the hills by tunnel. The city built the canal in 1890 to bring water and power back after the capital left.
Follow it south: it crosses Nanzen-ji on a brick bridge. People are always surprised to see one in a Zen temple.

npcs.name: Sumire すみれ
idle: The incline is my favourite in April: the cherries close over the rails like a tunnel.
The old boats rode up here on cradles. There's one still sitting on its cradle halfway down.

lines.title: Report back
lines.on_open: Both walks done. Walk back up the path to Haruka, at the bridge below Ginkaku-ji.

quests.title: Down the canal
talk: おこしやす. This is the start of the Philosopher's Path. The canal runs south along the hills for about two kilometres.

Two people to find along it, in either order. Mr. Kenji kept this canal all his working life: he's near Nyakuoji, where the path ends. And Sumire photographs the old boat railway at Keage, beyond Nanzen-ji. WASD to walk, Shift to run, E to talk. Who first?

choices.text: The water: Mr. Kenji, near Nyakuoji

quests.title: Where the water goes
talk: Walked down from Ginkaku-ji, have you? Then you've followed my water the wrong way: it runs north. It comes from Lake Biwa, through the hills by tunnel, and it has one more trick before it gets here.
Follow the canal on south into Nanzen-ji. Behind the great gate it crosses the temple grounds on a bridge of brick arches, the Suirokaku. Go and stand under it.

steps.text: Stand under the brick aqueduct in Nanzen-ji

quests.title: The great gate
talk: You walked the whole canal to get here? Then you've earned the short version. These rails carried boats, not trains: up from the canal on cradles, 582 metres of slope.
Now go back as far as Nanzen-ji and stand under the Sanmon, the great gate. Twenty-two metres of timber, built in 1628. I want to know whether you look up or look through.

quests.title: The poem on the stone
talk: おかえりやす. So: a canal that runs the wrong way, a brick bridge in a Zen temple, and a railway for boats. Not what you expected from a path about thinking, is it?
Nishida left a poem on a stone partway down. 'Others are others, I am myself; come what may, I go the way I go.' You've just walked it. That's the whole course.
